stimulus.title: A scale in an elevator
stimulus.html: A student of mass m stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator. The elevator starts at rest at the ground floor. From t = 0 to t = 2.0 s it speeds up upward with a constant acceleration of size a. From 2.0 s to 8.0 s it moves upward at a constant speed. From 8.0 s to 10.0 s it slows to a stop with an acceleration of the same size a. Air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Sketch a graph of the elevator's velocity against time from t = 0 to t = 10.0 s, taking upward as positive. Label the times 2.0 s, 8.0 s and 10.0 s.

rubric.point: A straight line rising from zero from 0 to 2.0 s
accept: a line from the origin with positive slope that ends at 2.0 s
straight increasing segment starting at v = 0

rubric.point: A horizontal line at a positive velocity from 2.0 s to 8.0 s
accept: flat segment above the axis, joined to the first
constant positive velocity in the middle interval

rubric.point: A straight line falling to zero at 10.0 s, with a slope of the same size as the first segment (opposite sign)
accept: symmetric decreasing line ending on the time axis at 10.0 s
the last segment is as steep as the first, sloping down

parts.sample: The graph starts at the origin and rises in a straight line to a positive value v_max at 2.0 s (slope +a). It stays flat at v_max from 2.0 s to 8.0 s. It then falls in a straight line to zero at 10.0 s, with slope −a, as steep as the first segment. The velocity never goes below zero.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the scale reading FN during the first 2.0 s, in terms of m, a and physical constants. Begin your derivation by writing a fundamental physics principle or an equation from the reference information.

rubric.point: Starts from Newton's second law applied to the student: ΣF = ma
accept: F_net = ma written for the student

rubric.point: Writes the forces with correct signs: F_N − mg = ma (up positive)
accept: F_N up and mg down in the sum

parts.sample: Newton's second law for the student, up positive: ΣF = ma. Two forces act on her: F_N (scale on student, up) and mg (Earth on student, down). So F_N − mg = ma, which gives F_N = m(g + a).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the scale readings during the first 2.0 s and during the last 2.0 s for m = 60 kg and a = 1.5 m/s². Use g = 9.8 m/s².

rubric.point: Speeding up: F_N = m(g + a) = 680 N (accept 678 N, or 690 N with g = 10 m/s²)
Slowing on the way up (acceleration down): F_N = m(g − a) = 500 N (accept 498 N, or 510 N with g = 10 m/s²)
accept: uses g − a for the last interval

parts.sample: First 2.0 s: F_N = m(g + a) = 60 kg × (9.8 + 1.5) m/s² = 678 N ≈ 680 N. Last 2.0 s the elevator still moves up but slows, so its acceleration points down: F_N = m(g − a) = 60 kg × (9.8 − 1.5) m/s² = 498 N ≈ 500 N.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A classmate claims: "From 2.0 s to 8.0 s the elevator is moving up, so the scale must read more than mg." Do you agree or disagree? Justify your answer.

rubric.point: Disagrees: the scale reads exactly mg
accept: the reading equals the weight in the middle interval

rubric.point: Justifies with the zero acceleration: constant velocity, so the net force is zero and F_N = mg (first law or second law with a = 0)
accept: the slope of the velocity graph is zero there, so ΣF = 0
moving up does not need a net upward force

parts.sample: I disagree. From 2.0 s to 8.0 s the velocity is constant (the graph is flat), so the acceleration is zero. By Newton's second law the net force on the student is then zero, so F_N − mg = 0 and the scale reads exactly mg. Moving upward does not require a net upward force; only speeding up upward does.
